lines.text: Customer-driven delivery. Work done because a specific customer, account or customer commitment asked for it. Counts: a feature, enhancement, integration or configuration that names a customer, account, deal, contract or customer deadline as its reason; a repair or other change whose stated reason is the request, escalation or deadline of a named customer (the repair is then also Bug fixes). Not this category: a feature with no named customer driver (that is Roadmap features); answering or troubleshooting for a customer with no change to the product (that is User support); a customer named only as an example or as one affected user, with no request or commitment.

Enablement and platform. New capability for people who build software: engineers inside the organisation, or external developers who build on the product's SDK or API. Counts: a new internal tool, command line tool, shared library, SDK or integration API; new build, deploy, environment or developer-workflow capability, and platform services that let other teams build. Not this category: a feature of the product itself, also when the users of the product are engineers (that is Roadmap features); tests and test infrastructure (that is Testing); moving to a newer version of a dependency, runtime or platform (that is Upgrades and migrations); routine release, build or deploy chores that add no capability (that is On-call and operational toil).

Roadmap features. New capability or enhancement for end users, with no specific customer as the stated driver. Counts: a new end-user feature, screen, workflow, report or public product behaviour; an enhancement of an end-user feature, and data or schema work tied to a new feature. Not this category: capability for people who build software (tools, SDKs, platform, pipelines) (that is Enablement and platform); work that names a specific customer as its reason (that is Customer-driven delivery); restoring behaviour that was already intended (that is Bug fixes); restructuring with the same behaviour (that is Refactoring).

Technical debt pay-down. Paying down a known accumulated liability in the code or system. Counts: removal of dead, deprecated or legacy code paths, stale feature flags, shims and workarounds; completion of postponed clean-up, replacement of a known shortcut, retirement of an internal legacy component that the text states as a liability. Not this category: restructuring with the same behaviour and no stated liability (that is Refactoring); a version bump, port or migration onto a newer or different platform, when the text states no liability (that is Upgrades and migrations); repair of a defect (that is Bug fixes).

Refactoring. Restructuring existing code with no intended change in behaviour. Counts: rename, extract, move, split, merge or simplify code; reorganise modules, remove duplication, tidy types or interfaces; lint, format and code-style clean-up with the same behaviour. Not this category: removal of legacy or deprecated code, workarounds or shims that the text states as a liability (that is Technical debt pay-down); moving to a newer version of a dependency, runtime or platform (that is Upgrades and migrations); a change that corrects wrong behaviour (that is Bug fixes); a change that adds behaviour.

Upgrades and migrations. Moving to a newer version or a replacement of a dependency, runtime, framework, platform or infrastructure, and the migration work it needs. Counts: dependency, lockfile, language, runtime, framework, database engine or infrastructure version changes; a port, rewrite or migration onto a different runtime, framework, language, platform or replacement service. Not this category: a version bump whose stated reason is a specific known vulnerability; upgrade is then secondary at most (that is Vulnerability remediation); removal of internal legacy code with no move to a newer version or platform (that is Technical debt pay-down); schema or data migration for a new feature (that is Roadmap features).

Incident response. Work to mitigate or resolve a specific production incident or outage that is active or has just occurred. Counts: a hotfix, rollback, mitigation or emergency restore that the text ties to an incident or outage; a change whose stated reason is a named incident, outage, severity level or page, and the review or write-up of that incident. Not this category: a defect repair with no incident or outage context (that is Bug fixes); a system change to prevent recurrence after the incident is over (that is Reliability); routine alerts, runbooks and operational chores (that is On-call and operational toil); a request raised by a user or customer (that is User support).

On-call and operational toil. Routine operational duty and manual toil outside a named incident. Counts: routine alert handling, threshold tuning of existing alerts, runbook steps, manual operational tasks and data corrections; routine scheduled rotation of certificates or keys, and routine release, build or deploy chores. Not this category: work tied to a named incident or outage (that is Incident response); a request raised by a user or customer (that is User support); a system change that removes a failure mode, and new monitoring or alerting (that is Reliability); a change in how secrets, certificates or access are handled (that is Security hardening).

User support. Helping a user or customer with the existing product: tickets, questions, troubleshooting and requests. Counts: investigation or troubleshooting of a problem that a user or customer reported; answers to questions, how-to guidance, account or data requests, a support ticket as the unit of work. Not this category: the code change that repairs a confirmed defect (that is Bug fixes); a product change that a named customer asked for (that is Customer-driven delivery); alerts and chores that no user raised (that is On-call and operational toil).

Bug fixes. Correcting a defect: delivered functionality that does not behave as intended. Counts: repair of wrong output, a crash, a regression, a broken screen or a logic error; work whose type or description states a defect in existing behaviour. Not this category: a repair made to end a named incident or outage; bugfix is then secondary at most (that is Incident response); remediation of a security flaw (that is Vulnerability remediation); timeouts, retries or capacity changes with no functional defect (that is Reliability); the word 'fix' used for a typo, lint, format or style chore (that is Refactoring).

Reliability. Engineering that makes the running system more dependable: resilience, stability, availability and performance under load. Counts: retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, graceful degradation, capacity, scaling, performance or stability improvements; new monitoring, alerting or observability built to detect failures, and system changes that prevent recurrence after an incident. Not this category: mitigation of an active incident (that is Incident response); repair of a functional defect (that is Bug fixes); routine handling or threshold tuning of existing alerts (that is On-call and operational toil); tests (that is Testing).

Testing. Adding or improving tests and the infrastructure that runs them. Counts: new or improved unit, integration, end-to-end or performance tests, repair of flaky or broken tests; test fixtures, test data, test harnesses, coverage work, test jobs in continuous integration. Not this category: build, deploy or developer tooling that is not for tests (that is Enablement and platform); a change that makes the production system more resilient (that is Reliability); repair of a product defect; tests that only come with another change are secondary at most (that is Bug fixes).

Compliance. Work required by a regulation, standard, audit, certification, legal duty or contractual policy. Counts: work that the text ties to a named regulation or standard, for example GDPR, SOC 2, HIPAA, PCI or ISO 27001; audit evidence, data retention or deletion mandates, licence compliance, mandated reporting. Not this category: security hardening with no stated external requirement (that is Security hardening); remediation of a specific vulnerability (that is Vulnerability remediation); internal coding standards, lint rules or style rules (that is Refactoring).

Security hardening. Proactive security hardening and controls that are not tied to one specific known vulnerability. Counts: authentication, authorization or permission checks added or tightened as a control; encryption, a change in how secrets are stored or handled, input validation hardening, security headers, abuse rate limits, least privilege, security logging. Not this category: remediation of a specific identified vulnerability, advisory or scanner finding (that is Vulnerability remediation); work that the text ties to a regulation, audit or certification (that is Compliance); routine scheduled rotation of a certificate or key with no change of control (that is On-call and operational toil); a login or access feature for end users with no stated security purpose (that is Roadmap features).

Vulnerability remediation. Remediating a specific, identified security vulnerability. Counts: a fix or version bump that names a CVE, security advisory or security scanner alert; remediation of a penetration-test or bug-bounty finding, or of a reported exploit. Not this category: general hardening with no identified flaw (that is Security hardening); a routine version bump with no stated vulnerability (that is Upgrades and migrations); a defect that is not a security flaw (that is Bug fixes).
